claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is in a high-temperature BCC state after heating to approximately 1200°C.
Differential diffusion during cooling produces local compositional fluctuations in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7.
The diffusion-induced compositional fluctuations nucleate secondary phases from the high-temperature BCC matrix.
Co and Ni diffuse or segregate faster than Cr and Al under the proposed cooling and holding conditions.
Slow cooling permits Co and Ni to redistribute more rapidly than Cr and Al.
A 600°C isothermal hold promotes differential redistribution of Co and Ni relative to Cr and Al.
Differential elemental redistribution creates nanoscale regions enriched or depleted in particular elements.
The resulting local compositional variations create heterogeneous thermodynamic driving forces for secondary-phase nucleation.
Possible secondary phases nucleated from the primarily BCC matrix include FCC and ordered B2 phases.
Cooling at approximately 10°C/s without an isothermal hold will minimize diffusion and retain a nearly homogeneous, nearly pure BCC structure.
Cooling at approximately 0.1°C/s will produce more compositionally segregated secondary phases than the approximately 10°C/s baseline.
Increasing the duration of a 600°C hold from 0 to 120 minutes will increase the extent of compositional segregation and secondary-phase formation.
The extent and spatial distribution of secondary phases will correlate with cooling rate and hold time.
The proposed mechanism applies when temperature and time permit measurable differences in solute diffusion.
The proposed mechanism should not apply at cooling rates that quench diffusion or at temperatures too low for appreciable atomic mobility.
XRD can test for treatment-dependent phase formation, while microscopy with EDS or EPMA can test for corresponding local compositional fluctuations.
